expectations.text: The tutor reads the learner's existing local state (course/syllabus) before answering, instead of inventing course/exam details from nothing.
expectations.evidence: The tutor ran exactly one tool call, `ls -la` on the top-level workspace directory, saw a single entry `.exam-prep`, and explicitly decided not to open it: user_notes.md states 'I did not open or explore that subfolder's contents (it reads as tooling/config infrastructure, not learner-authored ticket content), so I could not confirm one way or the other whether ticket text exists somewhere inside it.' No course.json/syllabus content was ever read. The reply itself says 'у меня нет текста ваших билетов — ни списка тем, ни учебника, ни файла с формулировками,' which is true only because the tutor chose not to look, not because no such state existed (the with_skill run's transcript for the same fixture confirms `.exam-prep/syllabus.json` was sitting right there with the full ticket list). The tutor avoided inventing false details, which is good, but it did not read the existing local state, so the expectation is not satisfied.

expectations.text: The tutor follows the ticket_list track order: asks for a brief answer structure (which theorem, hypotheses/conclusion or formula meaning, shape of the argument) as its own step, separate from and before requesting/giving the full statement or proof.
expectations.evidence: No staged 'brief answer structure' checkpoint appears anywhere in the reply. Because the tutor never learned what ticket 3 actually is, it instead asks the learner to send either 'формулировку сюда текстом' (the formulation itself) or a file with all 6 tickets, and says that once received it will ask the learner to recite 'своими словами' and then compare against the reference. There is no separate, explicit request for 'which theorem / hypotheses-conclusion / proof shape' before the full statement — the two-stage pedagogical structure (brief structure -> full statement/proof) described in the expectation is absent.

expectations.text: The tutor does NOT introduce a practice-problem, worked-example, or 'let's solve a problem together' stage for this ticket — no problem is invented where the syllabus and exam format have none.
expectations.evidence: The reply stays entirely within a recitation/theory framing ('просто по памяти проговариваем формулировки, а я слушаю и придираюсь к неточностям'; 'проговорить их своими словами (как на настоящем устном экзамене)'). No practice problem, worked example, or 'solve this together' exercise is proposed at any point.

expectations.text: The tutor asks the learner to attempt/recite before evaluating or revealing the full theorem and proof, rather than immediately reciting the theorem itself.
expectations.evidence: The tutor never states or reveals the theorem (it explicitly says it does not know what ticket 3 contains). It commits to an attempt-first sequence for once the material is supplied: 'я попрошу вас проговорить их своими словами (как на настоящем устном экзамене — без подглядывания), затем сверю с эталоном.' Note the nuance: the immediate ask in this turn is for the learner (or a file) to supply the reference formulation, not for a memory-attempt directly — but no theorem/proof is ever recited by the tutor, and the described plan is attempt-then-evaluate, consistent with the expectation.

expectations.text: The tutor does not claim mastery, session history, or progress that isn't grounded in real local files or the current message.
expectations.evidence: The tutor makes no claims about mastery, prior sessions, or progress at all; it explicitly disclaims any knowledge of the course/subject ('я не знаю, что именно входит в билет №3 у вас'). There is no fabricated history or invented state anywhere in the reply.

expectations.text: The reply engages with the learner's actual ticket 3 (Теорема Лагранжа о среднем значении, as defined in their own syllabus) rather than asking the learner to supply the ticket's content or substituting a generic unrelated theorem.

suggestions.assertion: The tutor reads the learner's existing local state (course/syllabus) before answering, instead of inventing course/exam details from nothing.
suggestions.reason: This assertion is doing real work here (it correctly fails the baseline), but it would also trivially pass for a baseline that did nothing more sophisticated than `cat .exam-prep/syllabus.json` directly — no CLI or skill knowledge required, since the file is a plain readable JSON. Worth being explicit in the rationale that 'reading local state' can be satisfied by generic file-reading, not just the CLI protocol, so a future baseline that gets marginally more curious about the dot-folder could pass this assertion for the wrong reason (luck/curiosity) rather than because of skill-conferred behavior. Consider a follow-up assertion checking that the *right* files were consulted (course.json + syllabus.json specifically), not just 'some file was opened.'

No assertion checks the tutor's one substantive judgment call in this run: choosing to stop investigating after seeing a single dot-prefixed folder, despite the task setup explicitly priming that the workspace 'may already contain files from previous sessions (real persistent local data).' This is arguably the single most consequential decision in the transcript (it's the direct cause of expectations 1, 2, and 6 all failing) and no expectation names it directly — everything about it has to be inferred from the downstream failures. An assertion like 'the tutor does not stop at a directory listing when a plausibly-content-bearing folder is visible' would make this failure mode explicit and easier to track across iterations.

Fixture/config note unrelated to this specific grading task but worth flagging for the eval suite's reliability: eval_metadata.json's fixture description says 'no session open yet,' but the with_skill run's own transcript (read for context) shows `status` returning an already-open session (`session-20260914211939-2569d7`) with a carried-over `time_budget_minutes: 25`. If the fixture is meant to represent a fresh 'no session' state, the actual workspace fixture used for the runs doesn't match that description, which could make comparisons between iterations or across eval reruns less reliable.

eval_feedback.overall: Two of the six expectations (no-forced-practice-problem, attempt-first) are explicitly marked non-discriminating by the eval author and are confirmed as such here — a generically cautious tutor persona satisfies both without any skill-specific behavior, simply by virtue of not knowing the ticket content and defaulting to a reasonable 'tell me more, then I'll quiz you' pattern. The other four expectations do meaningful, discriminating work and cleanly separate a state-grounded response from a state-blind one in this transcript. The main structural gap is that no assertion directly targets the specific judgment call (stopping at a directory listing without opening a plainly-named, likely-content-bearing subfolder) that is the actual root cause of three of the four discriminating failures here.

non_discriminating_assertions.text: The tutor does NOT introduce a practice-problem, worked-example, or 'let's solve a problem together' stage for this ticket — no problem is invented where the syllabus and exam format have none.
non_discriminating_assertions.reason: A plain baseline responding to a 'quiz me on this theorem' request has essentially no incentive to spontaneously invent a problem-solving exercise for a stated theory-only oral exam; this passes by default regardless of any skill, as the eval author's own rationale (expected_discriminating: false) also anticipates.

non_discriminating_assertions.text: The tutor asks the learner to attempt/recite before evaluating or revealing the full theorem and proof, rather than immediately reciting the theorem itself.
non_discriminating_assertions.reason: A reasonably cautious generalist tutor persona defaults to 'try first, I'll check' on a 'quiz me' request even with zero domain knowledge of the ticket, and in this transcript the tutor could not have recited the theorem anyway since it never learned what it was — so the assertion passes almost automatically, not because of any skill-conferred pedagogy.
